title: Twin Melodies (with poem: A Friend Found in Music)

topics.title: Music: words of rhythm and melody

learn.hook: A tabla, a flute and a power cut: that's all it takes to turn a dark corridor into a concert!
points: The lesson 'Twin Melodies' is a play about Shruti, a young violinist who plays fusion music with her band, and her father, who loves traditional music. Music is at its heart, and the paired poem shows music as a friend.
Music words: melody (a tune), rhythm (a pattern of beats), tempo (the speed of music), lyrics (the words of a song), harmony (different notes sounding pleasant together).
Indian classical music has two main traditions: Hindustani, mainly in North India, and Carnatic, mainly in South India. A raga is a melodic framework; a tala is a rhythmic cycle.
Instruments can be grouped as string (sitar, veena, sarod), wind (bansuri, shehnai, nadaswaram) and percussion (tabla, mridangam, dholak).

Great Indian musicians: Ustad Bismillah Khan (shehnai), Pandit Ravi Shankar (sitar), Ustad Zakir Hussain (tabla), Pandit Hariprasad Chaurasia (bansuri) and M. S. Subbulakshmi (Carnatic vocal), the first musician to receive the Bharat Ratna.

example.q: Fill the gaps: 'The tabla kept a steady ___ while the sitar played a sweet ___.'
steps: A tabla is a drum, so it gives the beat: rhythm.
A sitar plays a tune: melody.

learn.reallife: From wedding bands to school assembly songs and festival bhajans, music is everywhere in Indian life.

items.q: Classical tradition mainly of South India

quiz.q: What is a melody?
options: A tune made of a series of notes
quiz.explain: A melody is a sequence of notes heard as a tune.
quiz.mistake: Confuses melody with tempo or with an instrument

quiz.q: What does 'tempo' mean in music?
quiz.explain: Tempo is how fast or slow a piece of music is played.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up tempo with lyrics or rhythm

quiz.q: What are the 'lyrics' of a song?
quiz.explain: Lyrics are the words that are sung.
quiz.mistake: Thinks lyrics means the tune

quiz.q: In Indian classical music, what is a tala?
quiz.explain: A tala is a repeating cycle of beats; a raga is the melodic framework.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up tala and raga

quiz.q: M. S. Subbulakshmi, the first musician to receive the Bharat Ratna, was famous as a:
quiz.explain: M. S. Subbulakshmi was a celebrated Carnatic vocalist.
quiz.mistake: Links her with an instrument instead of singing

quiz.q: The Carnatic tradition of classical music belongs mainly to which part of India?
quiz.explain: Carnatic music developed mainly in South India; Hindustani music mainly in the North.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Carnatic and Hindustani

quiz.q: Which of these is a percussion instrument?
quiz.explain: The mridangam is a drum, played by striking, so it is percussion.
quiz.mistake: Does not know how each instrument makes sound

quiz.q: Read: 'The power had gone out and the hostel was dark and silent. Then Tenzin began to strum his guitar. One by one, doors opened; someone tapped a steel plate, someone hummed along. By ten o'clock the corridor had become a concert hall.' What does the last sentence suggest?
options: The hostel was turned into a real theatre
Everyone joined in and made music together
Tenzin was asked to stop playing
quiz.explain: It is figurative: so many people joined in that the corridor felt like a concert hall.
quiz.mistake: Reads the figurative line literally

teach.ask: Gappu taps his beak: "What's the difference between rhythm and melody? They both sound like music to me!"
teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! Rhythm is the beat, melody is the tune. Dha-dhin and la-la-la together!
teach.nudge: Hmm, which one is the beat and which one is the tune?

topics.title: Friendship: idioms, phrasal verbs and relative clauses

learn.hook: Who is the friend you'd call first with good news? Friendship has its own special vocabulary!
points: Friendship words: companion (someone you spend time with), confidant (a person you trust with secrets), loyal (faithful), trustworthy (can be relied on), inseparable (always together).
Phrasal verbs: stand by (support), count on (rely on), fall out (quarrel), make up (become friends again after a quarrel), drift apart (slowly become less close).

Idioms: 'a friend in need is a friend indeed' (a true friend helps when you need it), 'thick as thieves' (very close), 'see eye to eye' (agree), 'break the ice' (start a friendly conversation in an awkward moment).
Relative pronouns join ideas: who for people (a friend who listens), which for things (the song which we sang), whose for possession (the boy whose sister sings).

example.q: Choose the relative pronoun: 'Ananya is the friend ___ always shares her lunch with me.'
steps: The word before the gap is 'friend', a person.
The gap is the subject of 'shares', and for people we use 'who'.

learn.reallife: Making a new friend on the first day of school, standing by a friend during exams or making up after a fight: friendship is daily practice!

games.title: Friendship idioms
pairs: Birds of a feather flock together
Stop being friends after a quarrel

items.text: Ravi is the boy ___ sister plays the veena.
The song ___ we sang together is my favourite.
A friend ___ listens is a real treasure.
This is the harmonium ___ belonged to my grandfather.

quiz.q: 'Real friends stand by you in tough times.' What does 'stand by' mean here?
options: Stand next to you in a queue
quiz.explain: 'Stand by someone' means to support them, especially in difficulty.
quiz.mistake: Takes the phrasal verb literally

quiz.q: Which phrasal verb means 'become friends again after a quarrel'?
quiz.explain: To make up is to end a quarrel and become friends again.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up 'make up' and 'fall out'

quiz.q: What does 'A friend in need is a friend indeed' mean?
options: A true friend helps you when you need it
quiz.explain: A real friend is one who helps when you are in trouble.
quiz.mistake: Reads 'in need' as describing the friend's own needs

quiz.q: Who is a 'confidant'?
options: A person you trust with your secrets
quiz.explain: A confidant is someone you can confide in, that is, share secrets with.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'confidant' with 'confident'

quiz.q: Choose the correct word: 'The girl ___ kite got stuck in the tree asked us for help.'
quiz.explain: The kite belongs to the girl, so we use the possessive 'whose'.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'who' where possession is shown

quiz.q: What is the antonym of 'loyal'?
quiz.explain: Adding dis- gives the opposite: disloyal.
quiz.mistake: Picks a synonym instead of an antonym

quiz.q: 'After changing schools, the two friends slowly drifted apart.' What does 'drifted apart' mean?
quiz.explain: To drift apart is to slowly lose closeness over time, often without a fight.
quiz.mistake: Confuses drifting apart with having a fight

quiz.q: Read: 'Aditya and Faiz argued over a cricket bat in Class 5 and stopped speaking. Two years later, when Faiz broke his arm, Aditya carried his bag every day for a month. Soon they were inseparable again.' Which phrasal verb describes the ending?
options: They looked down on each other
quiz.explain: They became friends again, which is 'made up'. 'Fell out' describes the start.
quiz.mistake: Picks the phrasal verb for the beginning of the story

teach.ask: Gappu sniffles: "My friend and I fought over a worm. Now what? Teach me some friendship words!"
teach.praise: Chirp! We'll make up, and from now on we'll stand by each other. A friend in need is a friend indeed!
teach.nudge: But how do friends become friends again after a fight? And what do real friends do in tough times?

topics.title: A Friend Found in Music: sound devices in poetry

learn.hook: Have you ever felt that a song understood you better than anyone? Poets call that a friendship too!
points: The poem in this lesson presents music as a companion that comforts and stays with us.

Sound devices make poems musical: rhyme (matching end sounds), rhythm (a pattern of beats), alliteration (repeated beginning consonant sounds), assonance (repeated vowel sounds inside nearby words, as in 'sweet green leaves') and onomatopoeia (words that imitate sounds, like jingle or dhum).
A refrain is a line or group of lines repeated in a poem or song, like a chorus.
Personification lets music act like a person: it can whisper, hug or hold your hand.
'Feeling blue' is an idiom meaning feeling sad.

example.q:
Read this original poem:
'When I am lonely, music comes
And taps my shoulder with its drums;
The flute-notes whisper, "Don't be blue,"
The sitar strums, "I'm here for you."
Dha-dhin, the tabla keeps the beat,
A friend that lifts my dancing feet.'
Find one example each of personification and onomatopoeia.
steps: Music 'comes', 'taps my shoulder' and the flute-notes 'whisper': these are human actions.
'Dha-dhin' imitates the sound of the tabla.
example.answer: Personification: 'music comes / And taps my shoulder' (also 'flute-notes whisper'). Onomatopoeia: 'Dha-dhin'.

learn.reallife: Many people play their favourite songs when they are tired or sad; music can feel like a friend who always understands.

games.title: Name the device
items: The violin wept in the corner

games.title: Sound devices: true or false?
items: In the original poem, music is presented as a friend.
Music comes, comforts and lifts the speaker, just like a friend.
Onomatopoeia words imitate the sounds they describe.
Words like buzz, jingle and dhum sound like what they mean.
Assonance is the repetition of consonant sounds at the start of words.
That is alliteration; assonance repeats vowel sounds.
A refrain is a line repeated in a poem or song.
A refrain works like a chorus.
End rhyme is rhyme between the last words of lines.
For example, 'comes' and 'drums' at the ends of lines 1 and 2.

quiz.q: 'And taps my shoulder with its drums.' Music is given a human action here. Which device is this?
quiz.explain: Tapping someone's shoulder is a human action given to music.
quiz.mistake: Calls any image a simile

quiz.q: 'Dha-dhin, the tabla keeps the beat.' What is 'Dha-dhin' an example of?
quiz.explain: 'Dha-dhin' imitates the sound of the tabla.
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise a sound word

quiz.q: What is assonance?
options: Repetition of consonant sounds at the start of words
Repetition of vowel sounds inside nearby words
A line repeated in a song
quiz.explain: Assonance repeats vowel sounds, as in 'sweet green leaves'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up assonance with alliteration

quiz.q: What is a refrain?
options: The first line of a poem
A line or lines repeated in a poem or song
quiz.explain: A refrain is repeated, like a chorus.
quiz.mistake: Confuses refrain with 'refrain from' meaning to hold back

quiz.q: What is the central idea of the original poem 'When I am lonely, music comes...'?
options: Music comforts the speaker like a friend
The speaker wants to learn the sitar
quiz.explain: Every instrument in the poem comforts the lonely speaker, like a friend.
quiz.mistake: Focuses on one instrument instead of the main idea

quiz.q: 'The flute-notes whisper, "Don't be blue."' What does 'blue' mean here?
quiz.explain: 'Feeling blue' is an idiom for feeling sad.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'blue' as the colour

quiz.q: In poetry, what is rhythm?
options: The pattern of beats or stressed syllables
quiz.explain: Rhythm is the beat we hear when a poem is read aloud.
quiz.mistake: Confuses rhythm with rhyme or structure

quiz.q: Which line contains alliteration?
options: The flute sang like a bird.
quiz.explain: 'Soft songs soothe ... soul' repeats the 's' sound at the start of words.
quiz.mistake: Confuses alliteration with onomatopoeia or simile

teach.ask: Gappu hums: "How do poets make a poem sound like music, even without instruments?"
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Rhyme, rhythm and sound words like dha-dhin make a poem sing. Music really is a friend!
teach.nudge: Hmm, but which tricks with sounds make the poem musical?
